planting.note: Direct sow in fall so winter rains establish seedlings, or plant nursery starts in fall to early spring, into lean, very well-drained, dry, sandy or rocky, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; California buckwheat is a foundational chaparral and coastal sage scrub shrub prized above nearly any other plant for the sheer volume and diversity of native bees, wasps, and butterflies its flowers support. Narrow, gray-green, needle-like leaves cluster along woody stems below rounded umbels of tiny white to pink flowers that bloom from late spring through fall and dry to attractive rust-brown seed heads that persist through winter and add off-season texture. It thrives on neglect once established, needing no summer irrigation and often declining if watered on the same schedule as lawns or border perennials nearby. Leave the dried flower heads standing through winter for seed-eating birds and structural interest, then lightly shape in late winter before spring growth resumes.

planting.note: Sow in fall so seed overwinters and cold-stratifies naturally, into lean, gritty, very well-drained, dry soil in full sun; sulphur-flower buckwheat is a widespread Rocky Mountain and Intermountain West native of dry, rocky slopes and open pine forest.

directions: Plant in gritty, lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; sulphur-flower buckwheat forms a low mat of rounded, gray-green leaves topped from early to midsummer by flat clusters of bright sulfur-yellow flowers on wiry stems, aging to rust-orange and copper tones that remain attractive well into fall and winter. It is an important larval host and nectar source for numerous native butterflies, including several blue butterfly species, and its persisting dried seed heads feed overwintering birds. Extremely drought and cold tolerant once established, it thrives in the same rocky, mineral, low-fertility soils that most garden perennials reject, making it a natural fit for rock gardens, dry slopes, and high-elevation xeriscape plantings. Avoid rich soil, fertilizer, and supplemental summer water, all of which shorten its life and cause floppy, less colorful growth.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost with a month of cold-moist stratification, or set out nursery divisions in spring, into very well-drained, dry, gravelly or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained, gravelly or sandy soil in full sun; firecracker penstemon is one of the earliest and most reliable hummingbird plants of the desert Southwest, sending up spikes of narrow, tubular, brilliant scarlet-red flowers in early to mid spring, often before most other perennials have begun growth. Evergreen to semi-evergreen basal rosettes of blue-green leaves persist through winter, giving structure to the border even out of bloom. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once established and largely deer resistant, needing little more than good drainage and full sun to perform reliably for years. Deadhead spent flower spikes to tidy the plant, and avoid heavy summer irrigation or rich, moisture-retentive soil, both of which lead to crown rot in this desert-adapted species.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost with a month of cold-moist stratification, into very well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Palmer's penstemon self-seeds readily once established and often behaves as a reseeding short-lived perennial.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, sandy or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Palmer's penstemon is one of the tallest and most fragrant of the native penstemons, sending up stout flower spikes 3 to 5 feet high packed with large, pale pink to lilac, snapdragon-like blooms with a distinctive sweet fragrance that carries well through the garden. Broad, gray-green, clasping leaves surround the base and lower stem, giving the plant a somewhat succulent appearance even before flowering begins in late spring. It readily self-sows in loose, disturbed, well-drained soil, often persisting in a planting for many years as a rotating population of new seedlings even though individual plants may be relatively short-lived. Cut spent flower stalks back after bloom if reseeding is not wanted, and avoid rich soil or regular summer irrigation, which shortens its lifespan.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs propagated from semi-hardwood cuttings in fall to allow root establishment through the rainy season, into well-drained, average to lean, neutral to slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants need little to no summer water.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and water only to establish, since summer irrigation on settled soil is the leading cause of root rot and premature death in this famously drought-adapted shrub. Blueblossom ceanothus is one of the showiest California native shrubs, producing a spectacular late-winter to spring display of dense, powder-blue to deep cobalt flower clusters that smother the glossy, dark evergreen foliage and draw enormous numbers of native bees. It grows quickly, often 2 to 3 feet a year while young, reaching large shrub or small multi-trunked tree size along the coast, and works well as an informal hedge, slope stabilizer, or specimen where its rapid early growth and long-term drought tolerance can be put to use. Prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since old wood does not resprout reliably, and avoid heavy pruning into bare wood.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall to take advantage of winter rains, or set out nursery starts in fall or early spring, into well-drained, lean, dry to average soil in full sun to partial shade along the coast.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun near the coast or partial shade inland; sticky monkeyflower is a resilient California chaparral and coastal scrub subshrub with narrow, sticky, resinous, dark green leaves and an extended bloom season of open-faced, snapdragon-like flowers ranging from cream and pale yellow through peachy orange to deep red-orange depending on the population. Flowers appear nearly year-round in mild coastal gardens, tapering off only during the hottest, driest part of summer, and are a favored nectar source for hummingbirds and native bees. It is drought-deciduous in harsh conditions, dropping leaves during severe heat or drought and flushing new growth with the return of cooler, wetter weather, so do not mistake dieback for plant failure. Lightly prune leggy stems after the main flowering flush to keep growth dense, and avoid regular summer irrigation once plants are established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs rooted from semi-hardwood cuttings in fall or early spring into well-drained, average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun on the coast or partial shade inland; bush anemone is naturally rare in the wild but adapts well to cultivated garden conditions.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun along the coast or partial shade in hotter inland gardens, watering occasionally through the first two summers to establish a deep root system; bush anemone is a naturally rare California endemic, restricted in the wild to a handful of Sierra Nevada foothill canyons, yet it performs reliably in cultivation across a wide range of climates. Glossy, leathery, dark evergreen leaves set off large, fragrant, pure white, anemone-like flowers with prominent golden stamens in late spring to early summer, creating a striking display against the deep green foliage. Once established it tolerates considerable summer drought, though it looks and blooms best with an occasional deep soak during the driest months rather than complete neglect. Prune lightly after flowering to shape and remove any winter-damaged wood, since it flowers on the previous year's growth.

planting.note: Sow in fall so the plumed, twisted-tail seeds overwinter and cold-stratify naturally, into well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; established plants tolerate severe drought, wind, and poor, shallow soil.

directions: Plant on a dry, rocky, well-drained slope or bank in full sun; alderleaf mountain mahogany is a tough, long-lived Rocky Mountain and Intermountain West foothill shrub with small, wedge-shaped, deeply veined leaves resembling alder foliage, evergreen to semi-evergreen depending on winter severity. Small, inconspicuous flowers in spring give way to the plant's real ornamental feature: clusters of feathery, silvery, corkscrew-tailed seed plumes that catch afternoon light through summer and fall, giving the whole shrub a soft, smoky appearance from a distance. Extremely drought and cold tolerant once its deep root system is established, it is browsed by deer and elk in the wild and provides valuable winter forage and cover for wildlife. Little pruning is needed beyond removing dead wood, and the shrub is essentially maintenance-free in the lean, rocky soils it prefers.

planting.note: Sow feathery-tailed seed in fall or set out nursery plants in fall to early spring into very well-drained, dry, sandy or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Apache plume is native to dry washes and mesas of the desert Southwest and Great Basin.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; Apache plume is a semi-evergreen Southwestern native shrub with small, deeply lobed leaves and a long, nearly continuous bloom of single, white, rose-like flowers from spring through fall. Each flower is followed by a distinctive cluster of pinkish, feathery, plumed seed tails that persist alongside the next flush of blooms, giving the shrub a two-toned, constantly changing appearance of white flowers and dusty-pink plumes at the same time. It is exceptionally drought, heat, and cold tolerant once established, thriving in the same lean, fast-draining, low-fertility soils that support native sagebrush and juniper communities. Prune lightly in late winter to remove dead wood and maintain an open, airy form, and avoid rich soil or frequent irrigation, which produces lanky, less floriferous growth.
